page.title: The insertion signature of NSP15
page.subtitle: Reading Bianco et al. · an evidence journey across two coronaviruses
page.description: Animated guide to Bianco et al.’s NSP15 preprint: a rare GFP lineage, limiting-dilution intuition, inferred RNA origins, and the selective loss of distal insertions.

sections.heading: 01 / How does a rare lineage make cells glow?
text: Bianco et al. · preprint, not peer reviewed. An out-of-frame GFP reporter starts dark. A rare frame-restoring indel lets infected cells fluoresce; the virus particle itself is not green. [Fig. 1]

cells.reading: Insertions: 8/18 WT; none >2 nt in inactive.

initial.note: Fig. 1c,d; Results 87–104. Selected isolates, not all viral genomes.

steps.text: A virus particle carries the reporter into a cell. When the GFP message is out of frame, the infected cell stays dark. GFP is a fluorescent protein: the cell can glow, but the particle itself is not green. This cartoon has no molecular timescale. [Fig. 1a]

A rare insertion or deletion can repair the grouping of the reporter message. The infected cell can then make functional GFP and glow green. A virus lineage carrying that genetic change can pass the reporter trait to newly infected cells. [Fig. 1a–c]

A green-positive well is a clue that at least one compatible variant is present. It may still contain several virus lineages. Finding a glowing well and recovering a separable mutant lineage are different steps. [Fig. 1b]

Both WT and inactive-NSP15 reporters yielded green-positive isolates (18 and 16 examined). Green alone is not NSP15-specific. Sequence analysis found insertions in 8/18 WT isolates and no inserts >2 nt in the inactive group. [Fig. 1c,d; Results 87–104]

sections.heading: 02 / Make a crowd easier to follow
text: The illustrative panel makes the crowd-to-wells idea visible. The adjacent evidence/limits panel keeps reporter selection, sequence confirmation, and the 8/18 denominator separate. This is not an experimental recipe.

cells.reading: Links a recovered phenotype to its reporter change.
Only GFP-restoring changes enter this screen.
8/18 is examined WT green isolates, not all genomes.

initial.note: Fig. 1b–d; Results 87–124. Wells are illustrative—not counts or probabilities.

steps.text: With many founders, a green-positive culture can include the rare reporter-restoring variant plus other lineages. The green signal does not identify every virus in that mixture. [Fig. 1b]
The schematic fans the mixture into nine example wells: empty, mixed, or single-looking candidates. These are illustrative outcomes, not counts, probabilities, or instructions. [Fig. 1b]

A single-looking well is a candidate, not proof of one lineage. The authors followed green-positive isolates and checked the reporter region’s sequence, connecting a recovered phenotype to its reporter change. [Fig. 1c,d]

This assay selects for changes that restore GFP. It misses other insertions and deletions, so 8/18 describes the examined WT green isolates, not all viral genomes. The next stage broadens the view with sequencing. [Results 87–124]

sections.heading: 03 / From reads to a testable interpretation
text: The reporter recovers selected green lineages. Sequencing surveys a broader set of insertion events. Follow the evidence from a read to a proposed explanation; each arrow adds a question, not proof of a mechanism.

panels.title: FIVE QUESTIONS · read the evidence in order

cells.b: Reads, matches, classes and reported rates.
Origin and mechanism are inferred, not directly observed.

steps.text: Sequencing produces reads; analysis identifies candidate insertions. This is broader than the GFP screen because a candidate does not have to restore that reporter. Technical artifacts remain possible. [Results 105–125]

Match an insert to a possible donor region and locate its recipient. The relationship defines classes such as tandem and distal. Longer matches reduce chance assignment; matching does not directly observe transfer. [Results 126–160]
Divide event counts by the corresponding number of virus-derived reads to compare datasets in cpm. Keep the length/mapping subset and dataset identity visible. [Fig. 2; Fig. 3]

Then ask which class changes with NSP15 activity and which controls challenge an artifact explanation. A mechanism is inferred from these comparisons; it is not supplied by a read alignment alone. [Discussion]

sections.heading: 04 / A selective loss of distal insertions
text: Bianco et al. • August 17, 2026 preprint • NOT PEER REVIEWED. In HCoV-OC43/fsGFP, inactive NSP15 is associated with fewer and shorter insertions. The strongest change is in the distal class.

panels.title: ACTIVITY CONTRAST · published rates, shared scale

initial.note: Fig. 2a. Medians summarize distributions; individual events are not shown.
Rounded virus-derived read totals; use reported cpm. Results 110–122.

steps.text: All insertions ≥2 nt: 33.9 versus 6.93 cpm, about 4.9×. This is a read-normalized event frequency, not the fraction of infectious particles. [Fig. 2a; Results 110–122]

comparison.caption: cpm counts unique insertion events per million virus-derived reads. Bars keep their published values; emphasis guides comparison, not change over time.

steps.text: Distal mapped insertions ≥11 nt: 16.7 versus 0.2 cpm. The ratio of rounded rates is 83.5×; the authors report 84×. The effect is much larger than the all-insertion comparison. [Fig. 2c–e; Results 143–160]

comparison.caption: The authors report an 84× distal contrast. Exact rounded rates stay labeled; the tiny inactive bar is 0.2 cpm, not zero.

steps.text: Tandem mapped insertions ≥11 nt: 0.98 versus 0.99 cpm. Their similar frequency is an internal contrast, but some tandem events may be amplification artifacts. [Fig. 2b; Discussion 370–381]

comparison.caption: Tandem rates are nearly unchanged. Some tandem signals may be amplification artifacts; distal and tandem use the mapped ≥11 nt subset.

steps.text: The overall median falls from 12 to 3 nt. Median length and event frequency answer different questions; neither alone proves how an insert was generated. [Fig. 2a]

comparison.caption: Overall median length: 12 nt (WT) versus 3 nt (inactive). A median is not an event frequency or a mechanism.

sections.heading: 05 / Where did the added material come from?
text: The illustrative panel separates source, recipient, and proposed transit. The adjacent evidence panel retains the published nested counts and source note. Dashed links mean inferred origin; only the last step animates a proposed transit.

initial.note: 12,063 / 13,816 = 87% of long inserts map with a perfect or near-perfect viral match. Results 126–135.

steps.text: Solid marks locate a matching source and the recipient’s unexpected patch. The source boundary is conceptual: mapping gives an inferred origin, not a direct view of fragment generation or transfer. [Extended Data Fig. 1b]

In WT, distal donor sites span the genome; recipient sites favor the 3′ region and the embedded reporter. The donor–recipient distance has a median of about 10 kb. In inactive NSP15, sites are more locally linked. [Fig. 2c–e]

Longer inserts improve source assignment: 12,063 of 13,816 WT inserts ≥11 nt (87%) map to the virus. Short matches are more likely to arise by chance, and mapping remains inferential. [Results 126–135]

Together, activity dependence and source/recipient patterns support the authors’ proposed fragment-generation model. The transit shown here was not observed. Incorporation remains unresolved; the chart does not establish a unique biochemical route. [Discussion]

sections.heading: 06 / A second virus, a different comparison
text: SARS-CoV-2 supports a related insertion signature. Keep the paired public dataset separate from the authors’ deeper WT-only dataset: preparation, read depth and sampled population differ.

sections.heading: 07 / What survives the artifact challenge?
text: Converging evidence strengthens the interpretation, but each assay sees a different subset. Clinical insertion counts are observations, not incidence or mutation-rate estimates.

sections.heading: 08 / Sources, provenance and the open question
text: A nuclease-associated insertion process is supported by several forms of evidence. How fragments become integrated, which events survive selection, and how often they matter in nature remain separate questions.
